definition: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two medium-mass nuclei, usually with two or three neutrons; the products are more tightly bound, so energy is released, mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments.
A self-sustaining series of fissions in which neutrons released by one fission cause further fissions; its rate is steady when, on average, exactly one neutron per fission causes another fission.
A rod of a neutron-absorbing material, such as boron or cadmium, that is raised or lowered in a reactor core to control the rate of fission.
A material of light nuclei, such as water or graphite, that slows fast fission neutrons through collisions, so they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 and cause fission.
The part of a power plant where the coolant from the reactor core transfers thermal energy to water in a separate circuit, turning it to steam that drives the turbine.
Thick layers of steel and concrete around a reactor that absorb the neutrons and gamma radiation escaping from the core.
